ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Ribbon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces ribbon through the card’s activity — making a colourful line collage — so the child’s picture gains lines with actual shape: loops, bends and swoops in 3-D.

What is this?

Ribbon is a narrow strip of cloth that bends, loops and holds a curve. It is shiny, floppy and impossible to draw a straight line with — which is exactly why it is interesting.

What does it mean?

Collaging ribbon teaches the difference between drawn lines and real ones: a pencil line looks like a curve, a ribbon IS a curve. Line vocabulary — loop, zigzag, squiggle — becomes physical.

What does the child need to know?

Ribbon lengths (a hand-span long works best), white glue or a glue stick, and a paper base. Shorter pieces glue flat; long ones insist on loops, which is fine.

Why this matters

Ribbon is often a first sewing-box encounter, and it carries pre-writing geometry: every letter shape the child will one day write is a line — straight, curved, looped — practiced here in ribbon.

What it teaches

Line vocabulary, bend-and-hold finger work, glue-then-place sequencing, planning (what will this line become?), and the big-motor bonus round: ribbon waving in the air.

Words to learn

ribbonbendloopcurvelinecollagewavetail

Say this to your child

“"Here is our ribbon — look how it bends! Swoop! Make a big loop... now a squiggle... now a zigzag! A dot of glue — press. Our ribbon stays exactly where we bent it. What is YOUR ribbon going to be?"”

Step by step

  1. Hold a ribbon high and make one big loop in the air — the shape test.
  2. Lay three ribbons on the paper and decide together what each one is: road? river? rainbow?
  3. Glue under the first ribbon — dots along its path — and press it down.
  4. Keep bending and gluing until the lines make a picture.
  5. Take the leftover ribbon outside and run with it — air lines count too.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a blue bow sits with two long tails — a bow is ribbon’s favorite trick: one pull and the whole thing tightens or lets go.

Ask your child

"Can a ribbon stand up straight?" (only for a second!) "What did your ribbon become?" "Which line is longer — the ribbon or the pencil line?" "Show me a loop with your finger."

What your child can say or do

Your child may ribbon-wave through the whole house wearing the leftover length like a tail, or glue loops so tall the page becomes a maze — follow the finger, find the exit.

Out in the real world

Gift wrappers, dancers (rhythmic gymnasts wave ribbon on a stick) and book binders all use ribbon’s bend. Every wrapped present with a bow on it is this lesson, tied.

Try it together

Line family: draw a pencil line, a crayon line and a marker line on one page, then glue a ribbon line beside them. Ask which line the finger likes best — the finger always votes ribbon.

Understanding check

Ask: "What can ribbon do that pencil cannot?" (bend for real, stand up) "Show me a loop." "What do we put under the ribbon before pressing?" (glue)

This lesson pairs with the Ribbon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.
